subtopic_detail: Post UTI imaging decision at 20 months per RCH
stem:
You are the paediatric ward registrar reviewing a 20 month old girl in outpatient clinic 6 weeks after her first culture positive urinary tract infection. She was treated in the community with oral trimethoprim sulfamethoxazole after her general practitioner sent a clean catch urine that grew Escherichia coli sensitive to trimethoprim.

She was systemically well throughout, defervesced within 24 hours of starting antibiotics, and has since been thriving. She had a normal 18 to 20 week antenatal morphology scan reported by her mother, with no antenatal renal tract abnormality documented. She has no family history of vesicoureteric reflux, has never had a febrile UTI before, is fully toilet trained by day, and is passing a good stream on the potty. Growth centiles and blood pressure today are both on the 50th centile for age and sex.

Her examination today is unremarkable and a repeat urine is negative on dipstick and microscopy.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 108/min; BP 92/54 mmHg (50th centile); RR 24/min; SpO2 99% RA; T 36.7 C
data_table.Examination: Well grown, unremarkable abdominal and genital exam
data_table.Investigations: Repeat urine microscopy and culture negative today
data_table.History: First febrile UTI 6 weeks ago; E coli sensitive to trimethoprim; defervesced within 24 h; normal 18 to 20 week morphology scan; no family history of VUR

lead_in: What is the most appropriate imaging plan?

options.text: Reassure and arrange no imaging; advise on prompt culture and treatment of any future febrile urinary tract infection episode and safety net for return
options.rationale: RCH advises no imaging after a single typical febrile UTI in a well thriving child aged 6 months to less than 3 years with normal antenatal monitoring; parents are counselled to seek review with any future febrile illness (Source: RCH CPG Urinary tract infection).

options.text: Arrange a dimercaptosuccinic acid renal scan at 6 months to look for cortical scarring and any evidence of pyelonephritic damage to the kidneys
options.rationale: Dimercaptosuccinic acid scanning is a NICE construct and is not part of the RCH imaging cascade; it should not be requested after a single typical UTI (Source: RCH CPG Urinary tract infection).

options.text: Arrange a micturating cystourethrogram to grade vesicoureteric reflux and guide any decision about continuous low dose antibiotic prophylaxis in this child
options.rationale: Micturating cystourethrogram is invasive, involves radiation and catheterisation, and is not in the RCH cascade after a single typical UTI in a child with normal antenatal imaging (Source: RCH CPG Urinary tract infection).

options.text: Arrange a renal tract ultrasound this week to look at renal size, exclude occult obstruction, and confirm no residual pelvicalyceal dilatation
options.rationale: Ultrasound is only indicated for atypical UTI features, recurrent UTI, or infants under 6 months without antenatal monitoring; a single typical UTI in a well thriving girl with a normal antenatal scan does not need ultrasound (Source: RCH CPG Urinary tract infection).

options.text: Start continuous low dose trimethoprim prophylaxis for 12 months and arrange imaging if any further culture positive UTI occurs during the treatment period
options.rationale: Prophylactic antibiotics are not recommended after a single typical UTI in this age group; the PRIVENT trial and RCH guidance restrict prophylaxis to selected recurrent UTI or dilating reflux (Source: RCH CPG Urinary tract infection).

explanation.summary: The RCH imaging cascade after urinary tract infection reserves renal tract ultrasound for atypical UTI, recurrent UTI, infants under 6 months without antenatal monitoring, or when there is a family history of significant renal tract disease. A single typical UTI in a well thriving child between 6 months and 3 years with a normal antenatal morphology scan needs no imaging. Dimercaptosuccinic acid scanning and micturating cystourethrogram are NICE constructs and are not part of the RCH cascade. Parents are safety netted for prompt review and culture of any future febrile illness.
key_points: Single typical UTI plus normal antenatal scan plus well child equals no imaging.
Ultrasound only for atypical, recurrent, under 6 months, or absent antenatal monitoring.
DMSA and MCUG are not part of the RCH cascade.
explanation.pearls: Confirm the antenatal morphology scan was actually done and normal before deciding not to image; a missed antenatal scan converts a first typical UTI in an infant under 6 months into an indication for renal tract ultrasound.

subtopic_detail: First line oxygen delivery in moderate bronchiolitis per RCH
stem:
You are the emergency registrar reviewing a 7 month old ex 39 weeker with 3 days of coryza and 24 hours of cough, tachypnoea, and reduced feeds. He is passing about half his usual number of wet nappies. He has no chronic lung disease, no congenital heart disease, and no immunodeficiency.

On arrival he is alert, has mild subcostal recessions, and has widespread wheeze with fine inspiratory crackles. He accepts small amounts of oral fluids from a syringe. Nasal suction is performed with mild transient improvement in work of breathing.

Pulse rate 158/min, blood pressure 92/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 62/min, SpO2 89% in room air, temperature 37.8 degrees C. A nasopharyngeal aspirate is sent. Chest x ray is not obtained. His weight today is 8 kg.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 158/min; BP 92/58 mmHg; RR 62/min; SpO2 89% RA; T 37.8 C
data_table.Examination: Alert; mild subcostal recessions; widespread wheeze with fine inspiratory crackles
data_table.Feeds: Approximately 50 percent of usual intake; half usual number of wet nappies

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial oxygen delivery?

options.text: High flow nasal cannula humidified oxygen at 2 L/kg/min titrated to a saturation target of 94 to 98 percent as an initial escalation
options.rationale: High flow is reserved for failure of low flow after a trial of 2 hours; using it up front increases admissions to higher care beds without reducing intubation (Source: RCH CPG Bronchiolitis; PARIS trial).

options.text: Nasal prong oxygen titrated at 1 to 2 L/min to a saturation target of at least 90 percent while continuing supportive feeds
options.rationale: RCH bronchiolitis guidance recommends low flow nasal prong oxygen at 1 to 2 L/min as first line, with an SpO2 target of at least 90 percent; higher targets and high flow are not first line (Source: RCH CPG Bronchiolitis).

options.text: Hudson mask oxygen delivered at 6 L/min titrated to a saturation target of 94 to 98 percent while awaiting review by the paediatric team on the ward
options.rationale: A Hudson mask at this flow is not first line and blunts assessment of respiratory effort and feeding; low flow nasal prongs are preferred (Source: RCH CPG Bronchiolitis).

options.text: Nebulised salbutamol 5 mg with continuous saturation monitoring before commencing any supplemental oxygen or feeding support pathway today
options.rationale: Salbutamol is not recommended in bronchiolitis under 12 months; RCH advises against routine bronchodilators regardless of wheeze (Source: RCH CPG Bronchiolitis).

options.text: Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1 in 1000 followed by observation for at least 3 hours before deciding on ongoing oxygen support and disposition
options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline is not routinely used in bronchiolitis and does not alter admission or length of stay; oxygen and feeding support are the mainstays (Source: RCH CPG Bronchiolitis).

explanation.summary: RCH bronchiolitis guidance is deliberately conservative on oxygen delivery: start with low flow nasal prongs at 1 to 2 L/min and titrate to an SpO2 target of at least 90 percent. High flow nasal cannula is reserved for failure of low flow after at least 2 hours. Bronchodilators and adrenaline are not routinely recommended. Feeding support, hydration and time are the other pillars of care.
key_points: First line oxygen is nasal prong 1 to 2 L/min.
SpO2 target is 90 percent, not 92 to 94.
High flow reserved for failure of low flow after 2 hours.
explanation.pearls: Reassess at 2 hours after starting low flow; a persistent SpO2 under 90 on 2 L/min, sustained tachypnoea over 60 with recessions, or feeding failure defines low flow failure and is the trigger for high flow escalation rather than the initial choice.

subtopic_detail: Dexamethasone dosing in mild to moderate croup per RCH
stem:
You are the emergency registrar reviewing a 2 year old boy brought in overnight with a 1 day history of coryza, hoarse voice, and a barking cough. He is settled on his mother's lap and has stridor only when upset. There is no drooling and he has been drinking sips of oral fluid.

He has no chronic respiratory disease, no cardiac disease, and no history of intubation. Immunisations are up to date. Older siblings have had similar symptoms this week.

Pulse rate 128/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 34/min, SpO2 97% in room air, temperature 37.9 degrees C. Weight today is measured at 13 kg. He has mild suprasternal recession at rest and a barking cough on examination.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128/min; BP 96/58 mmHg; RR 34/min; SpO2 97% RA; T 37.9 C
data_table.Examination: Settled on lap; mild suprasternal recession at rest; barking cough; stridor only when upset

lead_in: What is the most appropriate corticosteroid regimen?

options.text: Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for 3 days as an outpatient course of steroids with a review by the general practitioner in 48 hours
options.rationale: Prednisolone 1 mg/kg for 3 days has been shown to have higher representation rates than dexamethasone in croup and is not first line at RCH (Source: RCH CPG Croup; Cochrane).

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg as a single stat dose in the department and reassess symptoms after 2 hours before discharge
options.rationale: 0.6 mg/kg is reserved for severe croup with stridor at rest and marked respiratory distress; using it in mild to moderate cases overtreats without added benefit (Source: RCH CPG Croup).

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg as a single stat dose in the department and reassess symptoms after 2 hours before discharge
options.rationale: RCH advises oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg for mild or moderate croup, with 3 hours of observation after any nebulised adrenaline; 0.6 mg/kg is reserved for severe croup (Source: RCH CPG Croup).

options.text: Nebulised budesonide 2 mg as a single dose in the department and reassess symptoms after 2 hours before discharge
options.rationale: Nebulised budesonide is an alternative when oral intake is not tolerated; this child is tolerating oral fluid so dexamethasone orally is preferred and cheaper (Source: RCH CPG Croup).

options.text: Intramuscular dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg as a single stat dose in the department and reassess symptoms after 2 hours before discharge
options.rationale: Intramuscular dexamethasone is reserved for children who cannot tolerate oral intake; oral dose at 0.15 mg/kg is equivalent and less distressing (Source: RCH CPG Croup).

explanation.summary: RCH advises oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg for mild or moderate croup with 2 hours of observation before discharge. Reserve 0.6 mg/kg for severe croup with stridor at rest and marked respiratory distress. Prednisolone is not first line because of higher representation rates. Nebulised or intramuscular routes are alternatives only when the oral route is not tolerated. Nebulised adrenaline is added for severe cases and mandates 3 hours of post dose observation.
key_points: Mild or moderate croup: dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg orally.
Severe croup: dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg orally plus nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1 in 1000.
Observe 3 hours after last nebulised adrenaline; 2 hours after steroid alone.
explanation.pearls: Croup severity is scored on stridor at rest, retraction and air entry; if a child has only intermittent stridor when upset with mild recession at rest, that is moderate and 0.15 mg/kg is enough.

subtopic_detail: First line adrenaline dosing in anaphylaxis in a 4 year old per ASCIA
stem:
You are the paediatric emergency registrar called to the resuscitation bay for a 4 year old girl who developed generalised urticaria, facial swelling, wheeze and a hoarse cry approximately 10 minutes after eating a peanut butter sandwich at a birthday party. She has known peanut allergy on her ASCIA action plan and her mother forgot her EpiPen Jr at home.

On arrival she is anxious, drooling saliva onto her mother's shoulder, and has audible stridor and diffuse expiratory wheeze. Perfusion is preserved. There is no chest pain and she has not vomited.

Pulse rate 148/min, blood pressure 88/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 40/min, SpO2 93% in room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C. Her weight from her most recent well child check 3 weeks ago is 16 kg.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 148/min; BP 88/54 mmHg; RR 40/min; SpO2 93% RA; T 36.6 C
data_table.Examination: Generalised urticaria; facial swelling; audible stridor; diffuse expiratory wheeze
data_table.History: Known peanut allergy; ASCIA action plan; ate peanut butter sandwich 10 min ago; EpiPen not available
data_table.Weight: 16 kg at well child check 3 weeks ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first dose of adrenaline?

options.text: Adrenaline 100 microg intravenously as a slow bolus over 5 minutes with continuous cardiac monitoring before repeating the intramuscular dose
options.rationale: Intravenous adrenaline bolus in anaphylaxis is reserved for cardiac arrest or refractory shock and only in a monitored setting; the initial route is always intramuscular (Source: ASCIA Acute management of anaphylaxis).

options.text: Adrenaline 160 microg intramuscularly into the mid anterolateral thigh calculated as 10 microg/kg from her measured weight of 16 kg
options.rationale: Weight based arithmetic is discouraged for anaphylaxis in AU; ASCIA banded dosing avoids error under time pressure and matches the EpiPen strengths available in community use (Source: ASCIA Acute management of anaphylaxis).

options.text: Adrenaline 300 microg intramuscularly into the mid anterolateral thigh as per the ASCIA banded dose for a child over 20 kg body weight
options.rationale: The 300 microg dose is reserved for children 20 kg and over; using this dose in a 16 kg child over doses her by a factor of about 2 (Source: ASCIA Acute management of anaphylaxis).

options.text: Adrenaline 150 microg intramuscularly into the mid anterolateral thigh as per the ASCIA banded dose for a 10 to 20 kg child
options.rationale: ASCIA uses banded intramuscular adrenaline dosing: 150 microg for children 10 to 20 kg; a 16 kg child sits in this band and the IM thigh is preferred over any weight based arithmetic (Source: ASCIA Acute management of anaphylaxis).

options.text: Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1 in 1000 with high flow oxygen while awaiting arrival of the paediatric intensive care retrieval team
options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline treats upper airway oedema but is not a substitute for intramuscular adrenaline in anaphylaxis; delaying IM adrenaline increases the risk of biphasic and fatal reactions (Source: ASCIA Acute management of anaphylaxis).

explanation.summary: ASCIA uses banded intramuscular adrenaline dosing to remove drug arithmetic errors under time pressure: 150 microg for 10 to 20 kg (EpiPen Jr band), 300 microg for over 20 kg (EpiPen band), and 500 microg for adults. The intramuscular anterolateral thigh is the first route in every case. Intravenous adrenaline is reserved for cardiac arrest or refractory shock in a monitored setting.
key_points: 10 to 20 kg equals 150 microg IM.
Over 20 kg equals 300 microg IM.
Repeat every 5 minutes while symptoms persist.
explanation.pearls: Do not use 10 microg/kg calculations for community or emergency anaphylaxis dosing; the banded table gives an equivalent effective dose without arithmetic and mirrors the EpiPen strengths.

subtopic_detail: Full septic workup in an unwell 6 week old with normal inflammatory markers
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a mixed regional emergency department reviewing a 6 week old male infant with 8 hours of poor feeding, one bilious vomit as reported by his mother, and reduced tone that his father describes as him being unusually floppy in his arms. He was born at term by normal vaginal delivery and had an uncomplicated newborn stay. He has been fully breastfed and gaining weight until today.

On assessment he is difficult to rouse, has cool peripheries with delayed central capillary refill, and mottled skin. His anterior fontanelle is soft. He has no rash, no focal chest signs, and his abdomen is soft with no palpable mass.

Pulse rate 188/min, blood pressure 62/38 mmHg, respiratory rate 62/min, SpO2 95% in room air, temperature 36.2 degrees C rectally. Point of care venous blood gas: pH 7.28, lactate 4.9 mmol/L, base excess minus 8. Bedside blood glucose 3.1 mmol/L. Initial white cell count 6.2 x10^9/L (5.0-19.5), CRP 8 mg/L (less than 5), procalcitonin not available onsite.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 188/min; BP 62/38 mmHg; RR 62/min; SpO2 95% RA; T 36.2 C rectal
data_table.Examination: Poorly rousable; cool peripheries with delayed central CRT; mottled; soft anterior fontanelle; no rash
data_table.Investigations: VBG pH 7.28; lactate 4.9 mmol/L; base excess minus 8; BSL 3.1 mmol/L; WCC 6.2 x10^9/L; CRP 8 mg/L
data_table.History: Term normal vaginal delivery; uncomplicated newborn stay; breastfed; poor feeding 8 h; one bilious vomit

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Give oral paracetamol 15 mg/kg, admit for observation on the paediatric ward, and await the results of urine dipstick microscopy and blood cultures overnight
options.rationale: An unwell shocked infant under 3 months needs immediate resuscitation and empirical antibiotics; awaiting cultures overnight without intervention delays sepsis treatment (Source: RCH CPG Sepsis; RCH CPG The febrile child).

options.text: Give IV adrenaline as an infusion first because his perfusion is very poor, then take blood cultures, then commence IV cefotaxime and consider a 20 mL/kg saline bolus
options.rationale: Inotropes are added AFTER adequate fluid resuscitation (up to 60 mL/kg) fails to restore perfusion; using adrenaline before fluids and antibiotics inverts the sepsis pathway (Source: RCH CPG Sepsis).

options.text: Give a 20 mL/kg 0.9 percent saline bolus first, then take blood cultures once perfusion has improved, then commence IV benzylpenicillin and gentamicin as empirical therapy
options.rationale: Sequence at RCH is IV access, blood cultures, first antibiotic dose, then fluid bolus; cefotaxime is preferred under 2 months because gentamicin monotherapy misses Listeria and dosing is more forgiving than penicillin plus gentamicin (Source: RCH CPG Sepsis).

options.text: Withhold antibiotics because his white cell count and CRP are not elevated, admit for observation, and reassess with repeat inflammatory markers in 6 hours if he deteriorates
options.rationale: Inflammatory markers are insensitive in early sepsis in this age group and are not used to justify withholding empirical antibiotics in an unwell infant under 3 months; delay is a preventable cause of death (Source: RCH CPG The febrile child).

options.text: Obtain IV or intraosseous access, take blood cultures and blood tests, give IV cefotaxime, and give a 20 mL/kg 0.9 percent saline bolus over 5 to 10 minutes
options.rationale: RCH sepsis pathway: IV or IO access, then blood cultures, then IV empirical antibiotic within the hour (cefotaxime for under 2 months to cover Listeria and Neisseria), then 20 mL/kg 0.9 percent saline over 5 to 10 minutes and repeat to 60 mL/kg total (Source: RCH CPG Sepsis; RCH CPG The febrile child).

explanation.summary: RCH sepsis pathway in a shocked infant is a fixed order: IV or IO access, blood cultures, first IV antibiotic within the hour, then 20 mL/kg 0.9 percent saline over 5 to 10 minutes, repeat to a total of 60 mL/kg before considering inotropes. Under 2 months the empirical antibiotic is IV cefotaxime to cover Neisseria and Listeria. Normal inflammatory markers do not exclude sepsis in early presentation and must not delay antibiotics in an unwell infant.
key_points: Order: access, cultures, antibiotics, fluid, then inotropes.
Under 2 months: IV cefotaxime empirically to cover Listeria.
Normal WCC and CRP do not exclude bacterial sepsis in early presentation.
explanation.pearls: A hypothermic infant with lactate over 4 and delayed capillary refill is in cold septic shock; treat with warm fluid boluses and expect adrenaline infusion to be needed once 60 mL/kg has been given, not before.

subtopic_detail: Choice of rehydration route in moderate paediatric gastroenteritis per RCH
stem:
You are the paediatric ward registrar reviewing an 18 month old girl admitted with 3 days of vomiting and profuse watery diarrhoea. Her sister has similar symptoms at home. She is estimated to be about 6 percent dehydrated by weight comparison with a well child weight 2 weeks ago at her health check.

She has been offered oral rehydration solution 5 mL every 5 minutes with a syringe over the last hour by her mother but has vomited most of it back. She refuses further syringe feeds and cries when the syringe is presented. She is not floppy and remains interactive. She has passed a small amount of urine 4 hours ago.

Pulse rate 148/min, blood pressure 92/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 32/min, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 37.6 degrees C. Point of care blood glucose 4.4 mmol/L. Serum sodium 137 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), bicarbonate 18 mmol/L (22-32), urea 6.8 mmol/L, creatinine 32 micromol/L. Weight today is 10.4 kg (was 11.1 kg 2 weeks ago).

data_table.Vital signs: HR 148/min; BP 92/54 mmHg; RR 32/min; SpO2 99% RA; T 37.6 C
data_table.Examination: Interactive; not floppy; dry mucous membranes; capillary refill 2 s; small void 4 h ago
data_table.Investigations: BSL 4.4 mmol/L; Na 137; K 3.6; HCO3 18; urea 6.8 mmol/L; creatinine 32 micromol/L
data_table.Weight: Today 10.4 kg; 11.1 kg 2 weeks ago (6 percent loss)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate rehydration plan?

options.text: Nasogastric rehydration with oral rehydration solution at 25 mL/kg per hour for 4 hours with vital signs monitored hourly on the ward
options.rationale: RCH advises rapid nasogastric rehydration as first line for mild to moderate dehydration when oral has failed; 25 mL/kg per hour for 4 hours is the standard rapid rehydration schedule and works well in gastroenteritis (Source: RCH CPG Gastroenteritis).

options.text: Intravenous 0.9 percent saline plus 5 percent glucose at maintenance plus 50 percent for 24 hours with 6 hourly electrolyte review through the admission
options.rationale: IV fluids are reserved for severe dehydration, shock or NGT failure; using them first in a moderately dehydrated child unnecessarily cannulates her and increases hyponatraemia risk (Source: RCH CPG Gastroenteritis).

options.text: Continue oral rehydration solution 5 mL every 5 minutes by syringe with encouragement from her mother and reassess her hydration status after 4 hours
options.rationale: Oral rehydration by syringe has already failed at 1 hour with ongoing vomiting; continuing the same failed strategy risks worsening dehydration and delayed reassessment (Source: RCH CPG Gastroenteritis).

options.text: Give a single oral dose of ondansetron 2 mg then retrial oral rehydration solution by syringe over the next 2 hours with hourly review by her nurse
options.rationale: A single dose of ondansetron 2 mg for 8 to 15 kg body weight is a reasonable adjunct but the primary rehydration route is still NGT if oral has failed; this option undertreats a 6 percent dehydration episode (Source: RCH CPG Gastroenteritis).

options.text: IV 0.9 percent saline 20 mL/kg over 30 minutes as a rehydration bolus and then reassess her hydration status before deciding on further fluid
options.rationale: A 20 mL/kg bolus is a resuscitation dose for shock; this child has no signs of shock and is not tachycardic beyond age norms, so a bolus is not indicated (Source: RCH CPG Gastroenteritis).

explanation.summary: RCH gastroenteritis guidance recommends rapid nasogastric rehydration as first line for mild to moderate dehydration once oral rehydration solution has failed. The standard schedule is 25 mL/kg per hour for 4 hours of oral rehydration solution via nasogastric tube. Intravenous fluids are reserved for severe dehydration, shock or NGT failure. A single dose of ondansetron helps reduce vomiting and IV need in the moderately dehydrated child but is an adjunct rather than a substitute for enteral rehydration.
key_points: NGT rehydration is first line when oral has failed.
25 mL/kg per hour of ORS for 4 hours.
IV reserved for severe dehydration, shock, or NGT failure.
explanation.pearls: Weigh the child on presentation and again during rehydration; using acute weight change is the most reliable bedside measure of dehydration and of successful rehydration in a child with recent well child weights recorded.

subtopic_detail: Severe croup management with concurrent adrenaline and dexamethasone
stem:
You are the emergency registrar called to see a 20 month old boy triaged with worsening stridor at rest and marked accessory muscle use. He has had 2 days of coryza and a barking cough. His mother describes him going floppy in her arms in the waiting room. Older siblings had similar symptoms without needing hospital care.

On arrival he is agitated when disturbed, has audible stridor at rest, intercostal and suprasternal recession, and appears tired between cries. He has no drooling and no rash. He is fully immunised.

Pulse rate 168/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 48/min, SpO2 93% in room air, temperature 38.4 degrees C. Weight today is measured at 12 kg. There is a barking cough and stridor is heard from across the room.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 168/min; BP 96/58 mmHg; RR 48/min; SpO2 93% RA; T 38.4 C
data_table.Examination: Agitated when disturbed; stridor at rest; intercostal and suprasternal recession; tiring between cries

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Nebulised adrenaline calculated at 0.5 mg/kg of 1 in 1000 plus oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg and observe for a minimum of 3 hours after the last dose
options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline is a flat 5 mL of 1 in 1000 per RCH; a per kg calculation is not the RCH protocol and dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg undertreats severe croup (Source: RCH CPG Croup).

options.text: Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1 in 1000 plus oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg now and observe for a minimum of 3 hours after the last adrenaline dose
options.rationale: Severe croup with stridor at rest and marked recession requires both nebulised adrenaline (flat 5 mL of 1 in 1000 by RCH; not per kg) and dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg, with 3 hour observation after the last adrenaline (Source: RCH CPG Croup).

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg alone with observation for 2 hours and safety netting for return if symptoms worsen at home overnight
options.rationale: Steroid alone at 0.15 mg/kg without nebulised adrenaline is not adequate for severe croup with stridor at rest; risk of airway obstruction is not addressed (Source: RCH CPG Croup).

options.text: Rapid sequence intubation now under paediatric anaesthetic support with an endotracheal tube one size smaller than would usually be predicted for age
options.rationale: Intubation is reserved for severe croup that fails medical therapy or shows impending respiratory failure; a trial of nebulised adrenaline and steroids is first (Source: RCH CPG Croup).

options.text: Heliox delivered by loose fitting mask plus intravenous dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg and observe for a minimum of 3 hours after the last dose of steroid
options.rationale: Heliox is not a substitute for nebulised adrenaline in severe croup at RCH; oral dexamethasone is equivalent to IV and less distressing than cannulation (Source: RCH CPG Croup).

explanation.summary: RCH severe croup pathway combines nebulised adrenaline (a flat 5 mL of 1 in 1000 per dose regardless of weight) with oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg, with a minimum of 3 hours observation after the last adrenaline dose to detect rebound obstruction. Steroid alone is inadequate for severe croup; intubation is reserved for medical failure or impending respiratory failure. Do not use per kg adrenaline arithmetic for the nebulised dose.
key_points: Severe croup: dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg PLUS nebulised adrenaline.
Nebulised adrenaline is a flat 5 mL of 1 in 1000, not per kg.
Observe at least 3 hours after last adrenaline for rebound.
explanation.pearls: Rebound obstruction typically occurs 2 to 3 hours after nebulised adrenaline wears off; discharge before 3 hours risks readmission with worse airway compromise, so treat the 3 hour observation as a hard rule.

subtopic_detail: Complex early neonatal jaundice with disconfirming DAT and normal groups
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar called to review a term female neonate on the postnatal ward at 30 hours of age with jaundice extending to the abdomen. Birth was uncomplicated at 39 plus 4 weeks by normal vaginal delivery to a G3P2 O positive mother. Rhesus antibody screening antenatally was negative. Cord bilirubin at birth was 42 micromol/L. The baby has been exclusively breastfed with adequate latch and has had 4 wet nappies since birth. Maternal serology is unremarkable.

On examination she is alert with normal tone, no cephalohaematoma, no bruising, and no organomegaly. There is no petechial rash. Both parents are of northern European heritage. There is a family history of splenectomy in the maternal grandfather in his thirties for unspecified reasons.

Serum total bilirubin at 30 hours is 285 micromol/L (unconjugated fraction 275 micromol/L; conjugated 10 micromol/L). Full blood count: haemoglobin 152 g/L (140-220), reticulocyte count 8 percent (elevated). Blood film reports frequent spherocytes and polychromasia with no fragments. Direct antiglobulin test is negative. Maternal blood group O positive; neonatal blood group A positive. Glucose 6 phosphate dehydrogenase activity is pending. Weight loss from birth is 3 percent. Baby is now under overhead single phototherapy while the team decides on further treatment.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 148/min; RR 44/min; SpO2 98% RA; T 36.9 C
data_table.Examination: Alert; normal tone; jaundice to abdomen; no cephalohaematoma; no petechiae; no organomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Total bilirubin 285 micromol/L (unconjugated 275; conjugated 10); Hb 152 g/L; reticulocytes 8 percent; film: frequent spherocytes and polychromasia, no fragments; DAT negative; maternal O positive; neonatal A positive; G6PD pending
data_table.History: 39 plus 4 weeks NVD; exclusively breastfed; 4 wet nappies; 3 percent weight loss; maternal grandfather splenectomy in thirties

lead_in: What is the most likely aetiology of this baby's jaundice?

options.text: ABO incompatibility haemolytic disease of the newborn presenting in the first 24 to 48 hours of life with brisk haemolysis with brisk haemolysis and reticulocytosis today
options.rationale: ABO incompatibility would be expected to give a positive direct antiglobulin test in most clinically important cases and the film is more likely to show microspherocytes without polychromasia (Source: RCH CPG Jaundice in early infancy).
source_refs: RCH CPG Jaundice in early infancy

options.text: Glucose 6 phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency causing oxidative haemolysis and the northern European heritage lowers this probability but the pending assay is required with reticulocytosis and DAT negativity
options.rationale: Glucose 6 phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency is X linked and rare in northern European girls; the film would typically show bite cells and hemighost cells rather than spherocytes with polychromasia (Source: RCH CPG Jaundice in early infancy).
source_refs: RCH CPG Jaundice in early infancy

options.text: Hereditary spherocytosis causing intracorpuscular haemolysis presenting on day one with unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and spherocytes on film with reticulocytosis and DAT negativity
options.rationale: Spherocytes on film with reticulocytosis, a negative direct antiglobulin test, and a family history of unexplained splenectomy is classic for hereditary spherocytosis presenting in the newborn period; DAT negativity is the key disconfirming finding for immune haemolysis (Source: RCH CPG Jaundice in early infancy; HSANZ Australasian hereditary spherocytosis guideline).
source_refs: RCH CPG Jaundice in early infancy

options.text: Physiological jaundice of the newborn accentuated by breastfeeding under intake in the first 48 hours of life with unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and no haemolysis on film today
options.rationale: Physiological jaundice does not present under 24 hours, does not cause reticulocytosis, and would not produce frequent spherocytes and polychromasia on film (Source: RCH CPG Jaundice in early infancy).
source_refs: RCH CPG Jaundice in early infancy

options.text: Cephalohaematoma resorption with delayed onset unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia; the film findings would be non specific and unrelated to the resorbing collection of blood on the scalp
options.rationale: There is no cephalohaematoma on examination and cephalohaematoma resorption does not cause frequent spherocytes; it typically peaks after day 3 (Source: RCH CPG Jaundice in early infancy).
source_refs: RCH CPG Jaundice in early infancy

explanation.summary: Hereditary spherocytosis is the leading cause of chronic congenital haemolytic anaemia in people of northern European heritage; presentation in the newborn period with early unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia is common. The diagnostic triad is spherocytes on film with reticulocytosis, a negative direct antiglobulin test, and a family history of unexplained neonatal jaundice, splenectomy or gallstones. The negative direct antiglobulin test kills the immune haemolysis differentials of Rh and ABO incompatibility. Confirmatory testing is by eosin 5 maleimide binding by flow cytometry or by osmotic fragility.
key_points: DAT negative haemolysis with spherocytes points to intracorpuscular defect.
Family history of splenectomy or neonatal jaundice supports HS.
Confirm by eosin 5 maleimide binding by flow cytometry.
explanation.pearls: When bilirubin is over the exchange threshold with haemolytic features in the first 24 to 48 hours of life, start intensive phototherapy first and send for HS confirmatory testing; folate supplementation for the first year of life is standard and up to a third of infants with HS require transfusion in the newborn period.

sources.label: RCH CPG Jaundice in early infancy

subtopic_detail: GDM diagnosis and immediate management on the 26 week OGTT
stem:
You are the antenatal clinic registrar reviewing a 32 year old woman at 26 plus 3 weeks in her second pregnancy who has just had her routine 75 g oral glucose tolerance test. Her first pregnancy was 4 years ago at a different hospital and she delivered by uncomplicated normal vaginal delivery at 39 weeks with a birthweight of 3.6 kg with no antenatal or postnatal complications.

Her body mass index at booking was 27. There is no family history of type 2 diabetes. She has been walking 30 minutes most days and is following the routine antenatal diet.

Her 75 g OGTT today shows: fasting plasma glucose 5.4 mmol/L (less than 5.1), 1 hour 9.6 mmol/L (less than 10.0), 2 hour 8.7 mmol/L (less than 8.5). Blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, urine dipstick negative for glucose and protein. Foetal fundal height is appropriate for gestational age today.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/72 mmHg; foetal fundal height appropriate
data_table.Examination: Booking BMI 27; walking 30 min most days
data_table.Investigations: 75 g OGTT: fasting 5.4 mmol/L; 1 hour 9.6 mmol/L; 2 hour 8.7 mmol/L (ADIPS thresholds 5.1 / 10.0 / 8.5); urine dip negative
data_table.Obstetric history: G2P1; previous NVD 39 weeks; birthweight 3.6 kg; no complications

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management plan?

options.text: Reassure that only one value exceeds the ADIPS threshold and repeat the 75 g OGTT in 2 weeks to confirm the diagnosis before starting any treatment
options.rationale: ADIPS criteria for gestational diabetes require only one abnormal value; repeating the OGTT would delay treatment without diagnostic utility (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines).

options.text: Diagnose gestational diabetes and commence subcutaneous insulin isophane 10 units at night immediately after this consultation with home capillary blood glucose monitoring 4 times daily
options.rationale: Insulin is not a first line agent without a lifestyle trial; it is reserved for lifestyle failure or immediate use if there is severe hyperglycaemia or foetal overgrowth already (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines).

options.text: Diagnose gestational diabetes and commence metformin 500 mg orally twice daily immediately after this consultation with monitoring capillary blood glucose 4 times daily as an outpatient
options.rationale: Pharmacotherapy is added after 1 to 2 weeks of lifestyle intervention if targets are not met; metformin first line without a trial of lifestyle is not the ADIPS pathway (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines).

options.text: Diagnose gestational diabetes, refer for dietitian and diabetes educator input, and commence home capillary blood glucose monitoring 4 times daily as an outpatient today
options.rationale: Any one abnormal value on the 75 g OGTT (fasting 5.1, 1 hour 10.0, 2 hour 8.5 or higher) diagnoses gestational diabetes; initial management is lifestyle plus home BGL monitoring 4 times daily (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines).

options.text: Reassure that all three values are below the diagnostic thresholds and continue routine antenatal care with a repeat OGTT arranged only if she develops any symptoms of hyperglycaemia
options.rationale: The 2 hour value of 8.7 mmol/L is above the ADIPS threshold of 8.5, so she meets diagnostic criteria and continuing routine care would miss the diagnosis (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines).

explanation.summary: The ADIPS Consensus Guidelines diagnose gestational diabetes on the 75 g OGTT with any one abnormal value: fasting glucose 5.1 mmol/L or more, 1 hour 10.0 mmol/L or more, or 2 hour 8.5 mmol/L or more. Initial management is dietitian and diabetes educator referral, education, and home capillary blood glucose monitoring 4 times daily (fasting plus 2 hour post prandial). Pharmacotherapy (metformin or insulin) is added if lifestyle fails to meet targets over 1 to 2 weeks or if severe hyperglycaemia or foetal overgrowth is already present.
key_points: One value at or above threshold diagnoses GDM.
Start with lifestyle plus home BGL monitoring.
Escalate to metformin or insulin if targets missed at 1 to 2 weeks.
explanation.pearls: Targets on home monitoring are fasting under 5.0 mmol/L and 2 hour post prandial under 6.7 mmol/L; use these for the metformin or insulin decision rather than repeating the OGTT.

subtopic_detail: Magnesium seizure prophylaxis in severe pre-eclampsia
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar on the birth suite at a tertiary centre reviewing a 28 year old primigravida at 34 plus 2 weeks referred from her general practitioner with new headache and epigastric pain. She had a blood pressure of 158/108 mmHg in the community and 162/110 mmHg on repeat 15 minutes later on arrival to the birth suite.

She describes a right upper quadrant ache and one episode of vomiting overnight. She has no visual disturbance and no chest pain. There has been no vaginal bleeding.

Pulse rate 96/min, blood pressure 162/110 mmHg confirmed on manual repeat, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C, foetal heart rate 140 bpm on CTG which is reactive. Urine protein to creatinine ratio 78 mg/mmol (less than 30). Platelet count 88 x10^9/L (150-400), alanine aminotransferase 128 U/L (5-35), creatinine 96 micromol/L (45-90). Reflexes are 3 plus with 2 beats of ankle clonus.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 96/min; BP 162/110 mmHg repeat; RR 18/min; SpO2 99% RA; T 36.8 C; FHR 140 bpm reactive CTG
data_table.Examination: Right upper quadrant ache; 3 plus reflexes; 2 beats of ankle clonus; no focal deficit; no visual disturbance
data_table.Investigations: Urine PCR 78 mg/mmol; platelets 88 x10^9/L; ALT 128 U/L; creatinine 96 micromol/L
data_table.Obstetric: G1P0 at 34 plus 2 weeks; new headache and epigastric pain

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Give intravenous methyldopa 500 mg as a stat dose and observe for 4 hours while awaiting placental function investigations to guide the timing of delivery decisions
options.rationale: Methyldopa is not an acute intravenous antihypertensive; onset of action is too slow for severe pre-eclampsia and the treatment does not cover seizure risk (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline).

options.text: Give oral labetalol 200 mg only and repeat blood pressure every 15 minutes with senior review if it does not drop below 160/110 mmHg within one hour of the dose
options.rationale: Antihypertensive therapy alone does not address seizure risk; magnesium is added when there are severe features or neurological symptoms, and IV rather than oral antihypertensive is preferred acutely (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline).

options.text: Give diazepam 10 mg intravenously as seizure prophylaxis and commence oral labetalol 100 mg while awaiting the consultant to make a decision about delivery
options.rationale: Diazepam is not the seizure prophylaxis of choice in pre-eclampsia; the MAGPIE trial established magnesium as superior with lower recurrent seizure rates (Source: MAGPIE trial; SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline).

options.text: Give a single dose of intramuscular betamethasone 11.4 mg and observe without other intervention because delivery is likely to be required within the next 48 hours
options.rationale: Antenatal corticosteroids are appropriate before 34 plus 6 weeks but do not address the immediate seizure and hypertensive risk; magnesium and antihypertensive are needed alongside (Source: RANZCOG Hypertension in Pregnancy).

options.text: Commence intravenous magnesium sulfate loading dose 4 g over 20 minutes then infusion 1 g/hour for seizure prophylaxis and treat the hypertension
options.rationale: Severe pre-eclampsia with neurological symptoms (headache, hyperreflexia, clonus) mandates seizure prophylaxis with intravenous magnesium; SOMANZ protocol is a 4 g loading dose over 20 minutes then 1 g/hour infusion (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline; RANZCOG Hypertension in Pregnancy).

explanation.summary: Severe pre-eclampsia with neurological symptoms (headache, hyperreflexia, clonus), thrombocytopaenia, or hepatic dysfunction requires seizure prophylaxis with intravenous magnesium sulfate. The SOMANZ regimen is a 4 g loading dose over 20 minutes then a 1 g/hour infusion, targeting a therapeutic level of 2 to 3 mmol/L. Acute severe hypertension is controlled with intravenous labetalol or hydralazine. Delivery is the definitive treatment after stabilisation and corticosteroids for foetal lung maturity before 34 plus 6 weeks.
key_points: Severe features plus neurological symptoms equals give magnesium.
SOMANZ regimen: 4 g load over 20 min then 1 g/hour infusion.
Diazepam is inferior to magnesium (MAGPIE trial).
explanation.pearls: Monitor magnesium clinically with 4 hourly reflexes, respiratory rate over 12, urine output over 25 mL/hour; if signs of toxicity stop infusion and give calcium gluconate 1 g intravenously over 10 minutes.
